rows.label: Card poster comments that were complaints

worked.note: The tip video engaged almost twice as well, and the card poster's comments show that a third of its audience used it to complain about card delays. The next card post should come after the delivery problem is fixed.

takeaways: A monthly calendar balances pillars and keeps slots free for news and outages
Every post with a rate, fee or promise is fact checked and reviewed before approval
Keep one warm, clear voice and adapt the tone to the moment
Every language version is checked by a native speaker, and posts are accessible
No unapproved investment promotion, no promised returns and no customer photo without written consent
Measure engagement rate, then read the comments to understand it

quiz.q: In Bank A's plan, 6 of 30 posts are fraud warnings. What share is that?
quiz.explain: 6 divided by 30 is 0.20, or 20%.

quiz.q: Who should review a post that contains an interest rate before approval?
options: Any colleague on the desk
Compliance or the product owner
Nobody, if the rate was in last month's post
The design agency
quiz.explain: Rates, fees and promises are checked against the approved source by compliance or the product owner.

quiz.q: Why should someone review the next 24 hours of scheduled posts every morning?
options: To increase reach
To change the brand voice
Scheduling tools delete posts after a day
A scheduled advert may no longer fit because of an outage or event
quiz.explain: Scheduled posts can become inappropriate when circumstances change.

quiz.q: A post reached 50,000 people and had 1,000 engagements. What is its engagement rate?
quiz.explain: 1,000 divided by 50,000 is 2%.

quiz.q: A customer agreed in writing to appear in a campaign for twelve months and asks for removal after six. What should the desk do?
options: Keep it until the twelve months end
Ask her to pay for removal
Remove it promptly
Blur her face and keep it
quiz.explain: Consent can be withdrawn, and the content should come down promptly.

quiz.q: Which wording is acceptable in a share offer post?
options: "30% dividend expected"
"Guaranteed returns"
"Buy before prices double"
Wording taken from the approved offer documents, with no promised return
quiz.explain: Investment promotion must match the approved offer and must not promise returns.

modules.title: Community management and complaints
modules.summary: Answer comments and messages on time and in the right tone, move private matters to secure channels, moderate by clear rules, escalate correctly and log every complaint.
objectives: Apply response time standards and measure the page against them
Reply in a calm, respectful tone using the SAFE method
Move account matters to secure channels without ever sharing or asking for account data in public
Moderate comments using written rules and escalate issues to the right team
Record social media complaints in the complaint register and track them to resolution

lessons.title: Response time standards
body: A response standard is the institution's promise about how fast it will reply. Bank A's policy sets four times: a first reply within one hour during service hours, a private follow-up within four hours, resolution or a clear update within one working day for simple matters, and complaint timelines that follow the bank's complaint procedure. Outside service hours, an automatic message gives the hours and the official call centre number.

The clock starts when the customer posts, not when the officer sees it. Measuring response time weekly shows where the desk is weak, usually evenings, weekends and the days after a campaign or an outage.

items.label: Within 1 hour
items.text: Public acknowledgement or first private reply

items.label: Within 4 hours
items.text: Private follow-up with the right team's input

items.label: Within 1 working day
items.text: Simple matters solved or a clear update given

items.label: Complaint timeline
items.text: Logged, tracked and closed under the complaint procedure

worked.title: Bank A response times after the evening shift was added

rows.label: Comments needing a reply this week

worked.note: The evening shift took the page from 45% to 80% on time, meeting the target. The six unanswered comments are traced to a weekend gap, which becomes the next fix.

lessons.tip: Measure from the customer's post time, and report the worst day, not just the average.

lessons.title: Tone that calms: the SAFE reply
body: Angry customers are usually worried customers: their salary is late, a transfer failed or the ATM did not give cash. A calm reply that recognises the problem lowers the temperature for everyone reading. Arguing, blaming the customer or posting a policy paragraph raises it.
Bank A trains its agents on a simple pattern, SAFE. It keeps public replies short and points the customer to a secure channel where the real work is done.

items.label: Say you hear them
items.text: Use their name and restate the problem in a few words

items.label: Apologise or empathise
items.text: Sorry for the trouble, without admitting facts you do not know

items.label: Find a secure channel
items.text: Invite a private message or the official call centre, never details in public

items.label: End with a next step
items.text: Say what happens next and when

example.title: A SAFE reply to an ATM complaint
example.text: Kebede Tolosa posted: "Your ATM in Bole ate my 4,000 Birr and nobody cares!" Yonas replied within 20 minutes: "Kebede, sorry to hear the ATM did not give you your cash. We want to fix this quickly. Please send us a private message with your phone number only, and our card team will call you today. Please do not share your card number or PIN with anyone. Yonas, Bank A." Kebede sent his number, the card team confirmed the failed dispense and the amount was reversed under the bank's procedure. He later posted: "Got my money back, thank you."

scenario.title: The sarcastic comment
scenario.situation: Under a new app feature post, Mekdes Haile writes: "Great, another feature, when the old ones don't even work. Three days and my transfer to my mother is still missing." Forty people have liked her comment.
scenario.question: Which reply is best?
options: "The app works fine for most customers. Please check your internet connection."
"Please share your account number and the transaction ID here so we can check."
Hide the comment so the feature post looks better
"Mekdes, sorry your transfer to your mother is still missing, three days is too long. Please send us a private message with your phone number and we will trace it today."
scenario.explain: The SAFE reply recognises the problem, apologises, moves to a private channel and gives a next step. Blaming the customer or hiding the comment angers readers, and asking for an account number in public breaks confidentiality.

lessons.title: Moving to private channels, never sharing account data
body: The most important rule on any bank page is simple: account data never appears in public, whether the bank posts it or asks for it. That includes account and card numbers, balances, loan amounts, transaction details, ID numbers and phone numbers. Even confirming in public that a person is a customer can breach confidentiality.

When a customer posts private details, the officer hides or removes the comment (and tells the customer why in a private message), and moves the conversation to a secure channel: the page's private messages for basic identification, then the official call centre, branch or secure app channel for anything that needs account access. Officers never ask for PINs, passwords or one-time codes, in public or in private.

regulation.source: NBE Financial Consumer Protection Directive (FCP/01/2020, as reported); bank secrecy obligations
regulation.text: The consumer protection directive, as reported, requires institutions to protect customer information, and bank secrecy obligations forbid disclosing a customer's affairs without consent or legal basis. A public reply such as "Your loan of 250,000 Birr is two months overdue" discloses confidential information to everyone who reads the page, even if the customer raised the subject first.

items.label: Public reply
items.text: Short SAFE reply, no details

items.label: Hide exposed data
items.text: Hide any comment with account or ID details and tell the customer privately

items.label: Private message
items.text: Ask only for name and phone number

items.label: Secure channel
items.text: Call centre, branch or in-app channel verifies identity

items.label: Close publicly
items.text: With consent, a short public note that the matter is resolved

scenario.title: The customer who posts everything
scenario.situation: Abebe Girma comments on Bank A's page with a photo of his bank statement, showing his full account number, balance and recent transactions, and asks why a 12,000 Birr deduction was made.
scenario.question: What should the officer do first?
options: Reply publicly explaining the deduction, since he shared the statement himself
Hide the comment, send him a private message explaining why and asking for his phone number, and pass the query to the account team
Leave it up so other customers can learn from the case
Ask him to post the transaction ID so the deduction can be identified
scenario.explain: Hiding the comment limits the exposure of his data, and the private message keeps the service going. Explaining the deduction in public would disclose his account affairs, and asking for more details in public adds to the harm.

lessons.title: Moderation rules: what stays, what goes
body: Moderation is applied by written rules that are published on the page, so customers know what to expect and staff do not decide by mood. Criticism and complaints stay up and are answered; deleting them looks like hiding and pushes customers to post elsewhere. Content that harms others is hidden or removed: personal data, scam links and fake contact numbers, threats, hate speech, insults aimed at individuals, and spam.
Each action is recorded in the moderation log with the reason, so the desk can show it acted fairly. Repeated abuse can lead to a ban, but only under the rules and with a supervisor's approval.

items.label: Keep and reply
items.text: Complaints, criticism, questions, negative reviews

items.label: Hide and message
items.text: Comments exposing the customer's own personal or account data

items.label: Remove and report
items.text: Scam links, fake numbers, impersonating accounts

items.label: Remove under the rules
items.text: Threats, hate speech, ethnic or personal insults, spam

items.label: Ban with approval
items.text: Repeat abusers, after a warning, logged with reasons

scenario.title: The abusive comment
scenario.situation: Under a post about a new branch, a user writes an insult about the ethnic background of the branch manager, who is named in the post. Other users begin replying angrily.
scenario.question: What should the officer do?
options: Reply defending the manager's background
Leave it, because deleting comments is censorship
Remove the comment under the published rules, record it in the moderation log, consider a warning or ban with supervisor approval, and inform the manager
Delete the whole post and all its comments
scenario.explain: Ethnic insults aimed at a person fall under the removal rules and may also engage the hate speech law. Arguing spreads it further, leaving it harms the manager and the page, and deleting the whole post removes legitimate comments.

lessons.title: Escalation: getting the right team involved
body: Social media agents answer many questions directly, but anything that needs account access, a decision or specialist knowledge goes to the owning team through an agreed escalation path. Bank A's escalation list names a contact and a backup for cards and ATMs, digital channels, fraud, branches, loans, human resources, and legal and compliance, with the time each team has to respond to the desk.

Some posts escalate straight to management: a claim the bank is failing, a post by a journalist or official, a viral video of a branch incident, a data leak, or anything mentioning a regulator. Agents do not reply to these alone; they alert the communications manager at once.

items.label: Classify
items.text: Question, complaint, fraud report, sensitive or crisis

items.label: Answer or route
items.text: Simple questions answered, others routed by the escalation list

items.label: Track
items.text: Ticket number and due time recorded

items.label: Chase
items.text: Desk follows up if the team is late

items.label: Close
items.text: Customer told the outcome, log updated

example.title: A transfer traced in a day
example.text: Mekdes, whose transfer to her mother was missing, sent her phone number by private message. Rahel opened a ticket for the digital channels team with a four-hour response time. The team found the transfer stuck in a failed status and reversed it to Mekdes's account. Rahel messaged her with the outcome and, with her permission, replied under the public comment: "Resolved with Mekdes, thank you for your patience." The public close reassured the forty people who had liked her complaint.

lessons.tip: Every escalated item needs an owner and a due time, or it becomes the next public complaint.

lessons.title: Recording social media complaints
body: A complaint made on social media is still a complaint. The consumer protection directive, as reported, expects institutions to have a working complaints procedure, to record complaints and to resolve them within set times. If the desk solves complaints in private messages but never logs them, the institution cannot see patterns, management cannot fix root causes, and complaint reports understate the problem.

Bank A now logs every social media complaint in the same register as branch and call centre complaints, tagged by channel and category. The monthly report shows where complaints come from and how fast they close.

regulation.source: NBE Financial Consumer Protection Directive (FCP/01/2020, as reported)
regulation.text: As reported, the directive requires a complaint handling procedure, recording of complaints, resolution within set times and information to customers on how to escalate. Complaints received on social media must enter this procedure like any other complaint, with a reference number given to the customer in a private channel.

worked.title: Bank A social media complaints, one month
worked.note: With every complaint logged, management can see that three in four social media complaints concern cards, ATMs, the app and transfers. The fix sits in operations, not in better replies.

visual.caption: Bank A social media complaints by category, one month (worked example)

takeaways: Set response times, measure from the customer's post time and fix the weakest hours
Use SAFE: say you hear them, apologise, find a secure channel, end with a next step
Account data never appears in public, and staff never ask for PINs, passwords or codes
Keep criticism, remove harm, and log every moderation action against published rules
Escalate through a named list with due times, and log every complaint in the register

quiz.q: When does the response time clock start?
options: When the customer posts
When the officer sees the comment
At the start of the next shift
When the team accepts the ticket
quiz.explain: Customers experience the wait from the moment they post.

quiz.q: What does the F in SAFE stand for?
options: Fix it publicly
Forward to marketing
Find a secure channel
Follow the customer
quiz.explain: F means moving the conversation to a private, secure channel.

quiz.q: Which item may an officer ask for in a private message on the page?
options: The customer's PIN
A one-time code sent by SMS
The online banking password
The customer's name and phone number so the call centre can call back
quiz.explain: Officers ask only for basic contact details; PINs, passwords and codes are never requested.

quiz.q: Which comment should normally stay up and be answered?
options: A link to a fake loan channel
A customer's harsh criticism of slow service
A threat against a branch employee
A comment showing someone else's account number
quiz.explain: Criticism stays and gets a reply; harmful content is removed.

quiz.q: Bank A closed 576 of 640 complaints within the set time. What is the rate?
quiz.explain: 576 divided by 640 is 0.90, or 90%.

quiz.q: Why must social media complaints be logged in the complaint register?
options: To meet the complaint procedure and let management see root causes
To identify customers for marketing
Only because the platform requires it
They need not be logged if solved in private
quiz.explain: Logging meets the consumer protection procedure and reveals patterns.

modules.title: Fraud, fake pages and scam warnings
modules.summary: Recognise how impersonation and investment scams work on Facebook and Telegram, spot fake pages, report and take them down, help victims safely and run regular customer warnings.
objectives: Describe how fake bank pages and scam Telegram channels deceive customers
Apply a checklist to tell an official account from a fake one
Report fake accounts to platforms and the right internal teams and track takedowns
Handle a scam report from a victim safely and quickly
Plan a regular fraud awareness campaign using the NBE instruction for microfinance institutions as a model

lessons.title: How impersonation scams work
body: Impersonation scams copy a bank's name, logo and posts to look official, then use the trust that comes with the brand. Common versions on Ethiopian social media include fake "loan support" pages and Telegram channels that ask for a processing fee, fake customer service accounts that reply under real complaints and ask for PINs or codes, fake job offers that charge application fees, and fake prize draws.

The pattern is almost always the same: catch attention, build urgency, move the victim to a private chat, and ask for money or secret codes. Knowing the pattern lets the desk warn customers in plain words.

items.label: Copy
items.text: Bank name, logo, photos and recent posts

items.label: Attract
items.text: Ads or comments promising loans, jobs or prizes

items.label: Rush
items.text: "Offer ends today", "account will be blocked"

items.label: Isolate
items.text: Move the victim to a private chat or phone call

items.label: Take
items.text: Ask for a fee, a PIN, a one-time code or a transfer

example.title: The "Bank A Loan Support" channel
example.text: In the running case, a Telegram channel named "Bank A Loan Support" appeared with Bank A's logo and copied posts. It promised personal loans of up to 200,000 Birr within 24 hours, with no collateral, for a 2,500 Birr "processing fee" paid to a mobile wallet. Within two weeks it had over 9,000 subscribers. Bank A's desk learned about it when Dawit Assefa, a teacher in Adama, posted on the real page asking why his loan had not arrived after he paid the fee.

lessons.tip: Real banks do not charge a fee into a personal wallet to release a loan. Say this in every warning.

lessons.title: Spotting a fake page or channel
body: Fake accounts often look convincing at first glance, but they fail simple checks. The desk teaches customers and staff the same checklist, and runs it itself whenever a new account using the bank's name is reported.
Some fakes are hard to spot, which is why the best defence is a single published list of official accounts and contact numbers. If an account is not on the list, it is not the bank.

items.label: Is it on the official list?
items.text: Compare with the accounts listed on the bank's website

items.label: Name and handle
items.text: Small changes: extra letters, "support", "official1", odd spellings

items.label: Account age
items.text: Created recently, renamed often, few old posts

items.label: Followers and comments
items.text: Sudden follower jumps, comments switched off, fake praise

items.label: Asks for secrets
items.text: PIN, password, one-time code: always fake

items.label: Asks for payment
items.text: Fees to a personal account or mobile wallet

scenario.title: Which account is real?
scenario.situation: A customer messages Bank A's page with screenshots of two Facebook accounts. One is "BankA Official Care", created three weeks ago, with comments switched off, offering to "unblock accounts" by phone. The other is the page linked from Bank A's website, active for eight years.
scenario.question: How should the officer reply?
options: Say both are official because they use the logo
Confirm that only the page listed on the website is official, warn the customer not to contact the other account or share codes, thank them, and report the fake account
Ask the customer to call the fake account to check
Reply that the bank cannot comment on other accounts
scenario.explain: The official list settles the question. Thanking and warning the customer encourages more reports, and the fake must be reported for takedown.

lessons.title: Reporting and taking down fake accounts
body: When a fake account is found, the desk captures evidence before reporting it, because fakes often disappear and reappear. Evidence includes screenshots, the account link and ID, the creation date, scam messages, and any wallet or account numbers used to collect money. The desk reports the account to the platform through its impersonation or brand reporting route, informs the fraud team and IT security, and, where customers have lost money, the fraud team works with law enforcement.

A takedown tracker records each fake, when it was reported, when it was removed and any repeat appearances. Wallet and account numbers used by scammers go to the fraud team so that they can be blocked or reported through the proper channels.

regulation.source: Computer Crime Proclamation (cited in the course specification as No. 958/2016)
regulation.text: The computer crime law, as cited in the course specification, makes unauthorised access to computer systems, computer-related fraud and related offences crimes. Fake accounts used to collect fees or codes from customers may be reported to law enforcement. The desk's job is to preserve evidence and work through the fraud and legal teams, not to confront scammers or hack their accounts.

worked.title: Bank A takedown tracker, one quarter

rows.label: Average days from report to removal
Wallet and account numbers sent to the fraud team

worked.note: Three in four fakes come down, but it takes five days and many come back. Takedown alone is not enough: customer warnings and a clear official list matter just as much.

lessons.tip: Screenshot first, report second. A fake that disappears before you capture it leaves no evidence.

lessons.title: Warning customers regularly
body: Regular warnings reduce fraud more than any single takedown. The NBE has set a clear model in its instruction on customer fraud awareness for microfinance institutions: monthly campaigns, fraud-warning messages in local languages, reporting of fraud-linked numbers and accounts, and reporting to the NBE within 10 days. Banks are not named in the instruction, but it is a useful model for any institution's page.

Bank A adopted a monthly fraud warning plan on its pages: one pinned warning updated each month, at least one fraud post every week in each main language, a short video every month, and an urgent alert within hours whenever a new fake is found.

regulation.source: NBE Instruction FCPED/142/26 (21 April 2026), customer fraud awareness campaigns by microfinance institutions
regulation.text: The instruction requires microfinance institutions to run monthly customer fraud awareness campaigns, send fraud-warning messages in local languages, report fraud-linked numbers and accounts, and report to the NBE within 10 days. For a bank's social media desk it is a practical template for the frequency, language and reporting of fraud warnings.

items.label: Every day
items.text: Pinned fraud warning and the official contact list stay on top

items.label: Every week
items.text: One fraud post in Amharic, Afaan Oromo and English

items.label: Every month
items.text: Campaign theme and short video, pinned warning refreshed

items.label: Within hours of a new fake
items.text: Urgent alert naming the fake account, with screenshots

example.title: A microfinance campaign done well
example.text: Gedeo Coffee Growers Savings, a fictional microfinance institution in Dilla, followed the NBE instruction with a monthly theme. In one month it warned about fake loan officers who collect repayments at homes. It posted a short Amharic and Gedeo language video, read the warning aloud on a local radio slot, and asked borrowers to report any such visit on the official number. Reports came in from three villages within a week, and the fraud-linked phone numbers were passed on as the instruction requires.

lessons.title: Helping a customer who has been scammed
body: When a customer says they have been scammed, speed and safety matter most. The officer replies publicly with a short, kind message and moves the customer to a private channel, then passes the case to the fraud team at once with the details the team needs: what happened, when, the amounts and the receiving wallet or account number. Fast action can sometimes stop the money moving further.

The officer must not blame the victim, promise a refund or discuss the case in public. The officer also reminds the customer to change any PIN or password they shared and to contact the call centre if their own account was accessed.

scenario.title: Dawit's loan fee
scenario.situation: Dawit Assefa writes on Bank A's real page: "I paid 2,500 Birr to your loan support channel on Telegram yesterday and nothing happened. Where is my loan?" He includes a screenshot of the wallet number he paid.
scenario.question: What should the officer do?
options: Reply publicly that the bank is not responsible for his mistake
Promise a refund of 2,500 Birr to calm him down
Reply kindly that the channel is fake, move him to a private message, pass the wallet number and details to the fraud team immediately, report the channel, and post a warning
Delete his comment so that others do not see the scam
scenario.explain: He needs help and the fraud team needs the wallet number quickly. Blaming him is cruel and bad for the brand, a refund promise may not be honoured, and deleting the comment hides a warning that protects others.

lessons.title: Investment scams and public warnings
body: Since the Ethiopian Securities Exchange opened, scam groups have new stories to tell: "pre-listing shares", "guaranteed daily returns from forex trading" or crypto schemes using a bank's or the exchange's name. Real offers are made through licensed capital market service providers and approved documents, and nobody can guarantee returns.

The NBE and the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority publish warnings about fake accounts and unlicensed investment schemes. The desk shares these official warnings on the bank's page, links to the original source and never adds its own claims about named individuals or firms without legal approval.

regulation.text: The Capital Market Proclamation regulates who may offer securities and provide investment services and prohibits market abuse. Promotions for unlicensed schemes are not legitimate offers. Sharing official NBE or ECMA warnings helps customers; making the bank's own accusations against named parties needs legal review.

scenario.title: The pre-listing shares group
scenario.situation: A Telegram group claims to sell "Bank A pre-listing shares" at 1,000 Birr each with a promised 50% return in three months. Customers ask the page whether it is real. Bank A has no share offer open.
scenario.question: What is the best response from the page?
options: Post a clear warning that Bank A has no share offer open, that the group is not official, that no one can promise such returns, and link any official ECMA or NBE warning; report the group
Say nothing, because shares are not the desk's responsibility
Ask the group's administrator to remove Bank A's name politely
Tell customers it is real but risky
scenario.explain: A clear, factual warning protects customers and the brand; the fake group should also be reported. Silence lets the scam grow, and calling it real is false.

takeaways: Impersonation scams copy, attract, rush, isolate and take
The published official list is the strongest test: not on the list means not the bank
Capture evidence, report to the platform and fraud team, and track takedowns and repeat fakes
Help victims quickly in private, pass details to the fraud team, never blame or promise refunds
Warn customers at least monthly in local languages, following the NBE fraud awareness model

quiz.q: Which request is a sure sign of a fake account?
options: A link to the bank's website
A request for a one-time code or PIN
A post about branch hours
A reply that uses the customer's name
quiz.explain: The bank never asks for PINs, passwords or one-time codes.

quiz.q: What should the desk do first when a fake account is found?
options: Message the scammer
Ignore it until customers complain
Capture evidence: screenshots, links, account IDs and wallet numbers
Post the scammer's personal details
quiz.explain: Evidence comes first because fakes often vanish and reappear.

quiz.q: 18 fakes were removed in a total of 90 days from report to removal. What is the average?
options: 5 days
4 days
6 days
18 days
quiz.explain: 90 divided by 18 is 5 days.

quiz.q: Which is NOT among the requirements of NBE Instruction FCPED/142/26 for microfinance institutions?
options: Monthly fraud awareness campaigns
Fraud-warning messages in local languages
Reporting fraud-linked numbers and accounts
Refunding every scam victim within 10 days
quiz.explain: The instruction sets campaigns, local-language warnings and reporting; it does not require refunds.

quiz.q: A scam victim posts on the real page. What should the officer avoid?
options: Moving him to a private message
Promising a refund publicly
Passing the wallet number to the fraud team
Reminding him to change any PIN he shared
quiz.explain: Refund promises may not be honoured and set false expectations.

quiz.q: A group sells "pre-listing shares" with a promised 50% return. What should the page post?
options: Nothing
A factual warning that no such offer exists, linking official warnings
A comparison of the group's returns with the bank's deposit rates
An invitation for customers to try it with small amounts
quiz.explain: A clear factual warning protects customers; promised returns are a red flag.

modules.title: Staff conduct online and the feed simulation
modules.summary: Follow the staff social media policy on personal accounts, confidentiality and political or ethnic content, then apply the whole course in the 15-post feed simulation.
objectives: Explain how personal accounts affect the institution and what the staff social media policy requires
Avoid disclosing confidential, customer or inside information online
Apply the hate speech and disinformation law to political and ethnic content
Report a colleague's or a page's harmful post through the right channel
Respond to a simulated feed of 15 posts with accuracy, the right tone and full compliance

lessons.title: Your personal account and the bank
body: Staff are free to use social media in their own lives, but customers, colleagues and journalists often know where they work. A post by an employee can be read as the bank's view, and a careless photo can reveal confidential information. The staff social media policy sets the line: personal opinions are personal, but staff must not speak for the bank, reveal confidential information, harass anyone or post content that breaks the law.

Only authorised staff speak for the bank. Everyone else who sees a customer question or complaint about the bank online should point the customer to the official page or call centre, not try to solve it from a personal account.

left.title: Fine on a personal account
items: Sharing the bank's official posts
Celebrating a work milestone without details
Personal hobbies, family, faith and culture
Pointing a friend to the official page

right.title: Not allowed
items: Speaking for the bank without authority
Photos showing screens, files or customers
Customer names, balances or loan details
Insulting customers, colleagues or groups
Posting rumours about the bank or others

example.title: The office selfie
example.text: On her first day at a regional office, a new teller posted a smiling selfie at her desk. Behind her, the screen showed a customer's name and balance, and a branch vault schedule was visible on the wall. A friend pointed it out within an hour, she deleted the post and told her supervisor, who reported it as a data incident. Bank A now tells every new employee: check the background before you post, or do not post from inside the branch at all.

lessons.tip: Before posting about work, ask: would I be comfortable if my manager and the customer saw this?

lessons.title: Confidentiality and inside information
body: Bank secrecy covers everything staff learn about customers: who they are, what they hold and borrow, and what they do with their money. It continues after a shift ends and after employment ends. Online, the risk comes from small leaks: a comment about "a big importer who just defaulted", a voice note in a group chat, or a document photographed for a colleague.

Staff may also learn inside information: unpublished results, a planned share offer, a merger or a large deal of a listed company. Sharing it, or trading on it, before it is public can breach capital market rules. Staff at banks with capital market subsidiaries need to be especially careful.

regulation.source: Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021; bank secrecy obligations
regulation.text: The Capital Market Proclamation prohibits insider dealing and market abuse, including passing on inside information about securities before it is public. Bank secrecy obligations forbid disclosing customer information without consent or legal basis. On social media, both apply to personal accounts, private groups and messaging apps as much as to official pages.

scenario.title: The group chat
scenario.situation: Yonas is in a private Telegram group with university friends. One asks whether it is true that a well-known Hawassa company is in trouble with its loans. Yonas knows from work that the company's loan is overdue and that a share offer by Bank A's capital market subsidiary is being planned for another client.
scenario.question: What should Yonas say?
options: Confirm the overdue loan because the group is private
Hint that his friends should wait for an upcoming share offer
Say he cannot discuss customers or anything he learns at work, and change the subject
Share a screenshot so his friends know he is not making it up
scenario.explain: Private groups are not private for secrecy or insider rules. Confirming, hinting or sharing a screenshot would disclose confidential or inside information.

lessons.title: Political, ethnic content and the hate speech law
body: Official pages stay out of politics: no party content, no comments on political disputes, and no content that favours or criticises any ethnic, religious or regional group. Bank A's customers come from every part of the country, and the page serves all of them equally.

Staff keep their own political views, but the law sets limits for everyone. Ethiopia's hate speech and disinformation law, as cited in the course specification, prohibits spreading speech that incites hatred or violence against people because of their ethnicity, religion and other protected characteristics, and spreading false information that can cause public disturbance. Staff who share such content can face consequences under the law and under the bank's policy, even when they only forward it.

regulation.source: Hate Speech and Disinformation Prevention Proclamation (cited in the course specification as No. 1185/2020)
regulation.text: The law prohibits hate speech against people based on characteristics such as ethnicity and religion, and the dissemination of disinformation that can cause public disturbance. For a bank, this means official pages remove such content under moderation rules, and staff must not create, post or forward it on personal accounts.

scenario.title: The forwarded video
scenario.situation: A colleague forwards a video to a staff WhatsApp group claiming that customers of one ethnic group are being refused loans at a named branch, with insults about that group. There is no evidence for the claim.
scenario.question: What should a staff member in the group do?
options: Not forward it, ask the colleague to delete it, and report it to the supervisor or the communications team under the staff policy
Reply with insults about the colleague's group
Forward it to more groups so that management notices
Post it on a personal Facebook account with a comment that it might be false
scenario.explain: The video may breach the hate speech and disinformation law and the staff policy. Forwarding or reposting spreads it even with a disclaimer, and responding in kind makes matters worse.

lessons.title: When you see something wrong
body: Every employee is part of the bank's early warning system. Staff who see a fake page, a scam using the bank's name, a viral complaint, a leaked document or a colleague's harmful post should report it, not argue online or try to handle it alone.

Bank A uses one internal email address and one phone number for social media concerns, monitored by the digital desk during service hours and by the duty manager at other times. Reports are thanked, never punished, even when they turn out to be false alarms.

items.label: Do not engage
items.text: No reply, no forwarding, no argument

items.label: Capture
items.text: Screenshot and copy the link

items.label: Report
items.text: Send to the desk's internal address or number

items.label: Protect
items.text: If customer data is exposed, tell your supervisor at once

items.label: Leave it to the owners
items.text: The desk, fraud, HR or legal team takes action

example.title: A teller spots a fake
example.text: A teller at Bank A's Mekelle branch noticed a customer showing her a Telegram message from "Bank A Card Desk" asking for a one-time code. She told the customer not to share it, took a screenshot with the customer's permission and sent it to the desk. Within two hours the desk had captured the channel, reported it and posted a warning in Tigrinya, Amharic and English. The teller's report was mentioned in the next staff newsletter.

lessons.title: The capstone: a feed of 15 posts
body: The course ends with a simulation. You take a shift on Bank A's page and respond to a simulated feed of 15 posts: complaints, scam reports, product questions and an abusive comment. For each post you choose an action (reply, hide, remove, escalate, report) and write or choose the reply.

Each response is scored on three things. Accuracy: are the facts right, the action correct and the right team involved? Tone: is the reply calm, respectful, short and in the customer's language? Compliance: no account data in public, no requests for codes, complaints logged, no unapproved promises or promotion. A compliance failure on any post caps that post's score, because one public disclosure can outweigh many good replies.

items.label: 5 complaints
items.text: Failed transfer, ATM cash not given, card delay, branch queue, fee dispute

items.label: 4 scam reports
items.text: Fake loan channel, fake care account, code request, pre-listing shares

items.label: 4 product questions
items.text: Savings rate, app feature, interest-free account, diaspora account

items.label: 1 abusive comment
items.text: Ethnic insult against a named employee

items.label: 1 data exposure
items.text: Customer posts a statement with account details

worked.title: Scoring one learner's simulation

rows.label: Posts with a compliance failure
rows.value: 2 (asked for a transaction ID in public; promised a refund)

worked.note: The learner passes the simulation comfortably, but the two compliance failures are the coaching points: never ask for details in public and never promise outcomes the desk cannot guarantee.

lessons.title: Rehearsal: three posts from the feed
body: Before the graded simulation, practise on three posts taken from a past feed. For each one, decide the action first and then the reply. Remember the order of priorities: protect the customer and their data, get the facts right, then get the tone right.
The fourth situation below is an example of what a strong learner did with a product question, so you can see a full-score reply.

scenario.title: Feed post 7: a code request
scenario.situation: A comment under a real Bank A post reads: "A man from Bank A called me and asked for the 6-digit code I just got by SMS so he can stop my card being blocked. Should I give it?"
scenario.question: What is the best action?
options: Reply: "Yes, if he gave his staff ID number"
Hide the comment because it makes the bank look bad

Reply quickly: "Please do not share the code. Bank A will never ask for it. Please send us a private message with your phone number, and call our official number if you shared it." Then escalate to the fraud team and plan a warning post
Reply that the desk will check with the card team tomorrow
scenario.explain: A fast, clear warning may stop the fraud in progress, and the fraud team needs to know. A staff ID proves nothing, hiding the comment removes a warning, and waiting until tomorrow may cost the customer money.

example.title: Feed post 11: a full-score reply
example.text: The post asked in Amharic: "Do you have an interest-free savings account and can I open it from the app?" The learner replied in Amharic within ten minutes: "Yes, Hana, we offer an interest-free savings account. You can start on the app under Accounts, Open new account, or at any branch with your ID. Full terms are on our website [official link]. Hiwot, Bank A." The reply was accurate (checked against the product page), in the customer's language, short, and linked to the official terms without promising anything not in them.

lessons.tip: Decide the action before you write a word: reply, hide, remove, escalate or report.

takeaways: Staff may post personally, but must not speak for the bank, leak information or harass anyone
Bank secrecy and insider rules apply in private groups and messaging apps too
Official pages stay out of politics, and no one creates or forwards hateful or false content
Report concerns to the desk instead of engaging, and capture evidence first
In the simulation, compliance comes first, then accuracy, then tone

quiz.q: Who may speak for the bank on social media?
options: Any employee who knows the answer
Anyone, if they add "views are my own"
Branch managers on their personal accounts
Only authorised staff on the official accounts
quiz.explain: Only authorised staff speak for the bank; others point customers to the official channels.

quiz.q: Is a private group chat safe for discussing a customer's overdue loan?
options: Yes, if the group is small
No, bank secrecy applies in private groups too
Yes, if the customer's name is not used but the company is described
Yes, after working hours
quiz.explain: Secrecy obligations apply everywhere, including private chats.

quiz.q: Under the hate speech and disinformation law, which statement is correct?
options: Forwarding hateful content is acceptable if you did not write it
Spreading speech that incites hatred against an ethnic group is prohibited
The law applies only to journalists
A disclaimer makes false content lawful
quiz.explain: The law prohibits hate speech and the spread of disinformation, including by forwarding.

quiz.q: A learner earns 52, 38 and 39 points of 150. What is the score?
A customer comments that a caller is asking for her SMS code. What should the page do first?
options: Tell her immediately not to share the code and move her to a private message
Ask for her account number to check
Wait for the fraud team's report
Hide the comment
quiz.explain: Speed matters most: stop the code being shared, then escalate.

quiz.q: What should a staff member do on finding a leaked internal document online?
options: Comment that it is fake
Share it with colleagues to warn them
Capture the link and report it to the desk and supervisor without engaging
Download and keep a copy at home
quiz.explain: Capture and report; the owning teams take action.

simulation.title: A week as social media officer at Bank A, head office digital desk
setting: You have just joined the digital desk at Bank A's head office in Addis Ababa as social media officer. Bank A is a fictional Ethiopian commercial bank with official Facebook, Telegram, TikTok and LinkedIn accounts in Amharic, Afaan Oromo and English. You plan and post content, watch the comments and work alongside two customer service agents who answer messages in shifts.

You report to the communications manager, who owns the pages and has set three goals for the quarter: 80% of comments answered within one hour, zero unanswered comments, and every social media complaint logged in the bank's complaint register. Fake 'Bank A' channels have been growing on Telegram, and the fraud team expects the desk to warn customers fast.
Every reply is read by far more people than the customer who asked. Items arrive in order and some choices come back later in the week. Decide the action first, then the words.

authority.title: Your desk's standards and rules

rows.label: Response times
rows.value: First reply within 1 hour in service hours; private follow-up within 4 hours; simple matters solved or updated within 1 working day

rows.label: Quarter goals
rows.value: 80% on-time replies; zero unanswered; 100% of complaints logged

rows.label: Content mix
rows.value: Product posts under a third of the plan; a fraud warning at least weekly; 4 free slots a month for news and outages

rows.label: Approvals
rows.value: Every rate, fee or promise checked against the approved tariff and reviewed; each language version read by a native speaker

rows.label: Privacy (FCP/01/2020, reported; bank secrecy)
rows.value: No account data in public, ever; never ask for a PIN, password or code; customer photos only with written consent

rows.label: Investment posts (Capital Market Proc. No. 1248/2021)
rows.value: Only approved offers in approved wording; no promised returns

rows.label: Fraud warnings (FCPED/142/26 model)
rows.value: Monthly campaign, warnings in local languages, fraud-linked numbers reported

rows.label: Staff conduct
rows.value: Only authorized staff speak for the bank; no confidential information on personal accounts or private groups

authority.note: These follow the course and the rules it cites. Your own institution's social media policy and compliance guidance always come first.

meters.label: Brand trust
meters.help: Rises with honest, calm and useful posts and replies; falls with silence, deletion, blame or misleading content.

meters.label: Customer service
meters.help: Rises when customers get fast replies and real fixes; falls with late, unanswered or unresolved cases.

meters.label: Fraud protection
meters.help: Rises when customers are warned and fakes are caught fast; falls when scams spread or customers are put at risk.

meters.label: Compliance
meters.help: Falls sharply with any public data exposure, unapproved promotion or missing consent; rises when rules are applied well.

tasks.subject: One improvement this quarter: which one?
body: The communications manager shares last week's page health report. She has budget for one improvement this quarter: a new design agency, a scheduling tool to push more adverts, or a second customer service agent for the evening shift. She asks for your recommendation with numbers.

exhibit.title: Bank A page health, last week

rows.label: Comments needing a reply, 8 am to 6 pm
Comments needing a reply, 6 pm to 10 pm

options.text: The evening agent: replies are 50% on time and evenings 15%; at 80% in the evening the page reaches about 76%. Log every complaint.
options.outcome: Correct: (264 + 36) / 600 = 50%, evenings 36 / 240 = 15%. At 80% in the evening, 264 + 192 = 456, or 76%. Only 84 / 210 = 40% of complaints are logged. The data points to evening capacity, not design.

options.text: The design agency: a fresher, more professional page will cut complaints, and better posts will lift the engagement rate across platforms.
options.outcome: A page is judged by its comment section. Better designs do not answer the 204 evening comments that missed the one-hour target.

options.text: The scheduling tool, and switch off comments after 6 pm so the evening backlog stops dragging the one-hour response rate down.
options.outcome: Turning off comments hides the problem and pushes customers to fake pages that appear to answer. More adverts do not serve anyone.

options.text: The evening agent, and report the projected 76% to the board as meeting the 80% target, since it is close and trending up.
options.outcome: The right choice, but 76% is short of the 80% goal. Report it honestly and name the next fix, such as weekend cover or better templates.

tasks.subject: Scheduled at 11:00: 'Save with Bank A at 7.5% a year'
body: Checking the next 24 hours of scheduled posts, you see a savings post set for 11:00 that shows last quarter's rate of 7.5%. The board approved new savings rates last week, but the product team has not yet sent the new figure in writing.
A product manager calls: 'Just change it to 8.5%, that is what was agreed in the meeting.'

options.text: Let it post at 11:00 as planned, and correct the rate in the comments and the next post if any customer asks about it.
options.outcome: Posting a rate the bank no longer offers misleads every reader and breaks the advertising and consumer protection duties. A correction in the comments reaches only a few.

options.text: Change it to 8.5%, the figure the product manager gave from last week's board meeting, and post on time at 11:00.
options.outcome: A rate from a phone call may also be wrong. Every rate in a post is checked against the approved tariff in writing before it goes out.

options.text: Pause the post, get the approved rate from the product team in writing, and reschedule it in one of the free slots.
options.outcome: Correct. Module 2: rates must match the approved tariff. A few hours' delay costs nothing compared with advertising the wrong rate to thousands of customers.

options.text: Delete the post from the calendar quietly so the wrong rate never appears, and move on to the next scheduled item.
options.outcome: The wrong rate does not go out, but the plan now has an unexplained gap and the product team never hears about the problem.

tasks.subject: Next month's plan: push the new debit card harder
body: The head of retail wants next month's Facebook plan to push the new debit card and has sent a draft. You notice it has no free slots and fewer fraud posts than the desk's standard.
Last month's card poster also drew complaints: 34% of its comments were about card delivery delays, which operations says will be fixed in about three weeks.

exhibit.title: Draft Facebook plan, next month (30 posts)

rows.label: Free slots for news and outages

tasks.ask: What plan do you send back?

options.text: Accept the draft: retail owns the card and its budget, and a strong card month will bring the page new followers.
options.outcome: 17 / 30 = 57% product posts, only 2 fraud warnings and no room for an outage notice. Customers stop reading a page that is half adverts, and the fraud warning never reaches them.

options.text: 26 posts plus 4 free slots: 9 product (30%), 6 tips, 5 fraud, 4 stories, 2 news; run the card push once delivery is fixed.
options.outcome: Correct: 9 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 26, plus 4 slots = 30, and 9 / 30 keeps product under a third. Promoting the card while a third of comments complain about delivery would only feed more complaints.

options.text: Keep the 17 product posts for the card launch but swap two of them for fraud warnings, so fraud appears four times.
options.outcome: Fraud warnings improve, but product is still about half the plan and there is still no free slot for news or an outage.

options.text: Drop the debit card from the plan entirely until operations fixes delivery, and fill the slots with financial tips.
options.outcome: The card is a real product customers want to know about. The answer is a balanced share and better timing, not silence.

tasks.subject: 'Three days and my transfer to my mother is still missing'
body: Under the new app feature post, W/ro Selam Tadesse writes: 'Great, another feature, when the old ones don't even work. Three days and my transfer to my mother is still missing.' Sixty people have liked her comment.
A new agent has drafted a reply for you to approve: 'Dear valued customer, please share your account number and the transaction ID here so we can check.'

options.text: Approve the agent's draft asking her to post her account number and transaction ID in the comments, so the team can trace it within the hour.
options.outcome: Account data never appears in public, whether the bank posts it or asks for it. Asking for it in the comments also teaches customers to post details that fraudsters read.

options.text: Reply: 'Selam, sorry, three days is too long. Please send us a private message with your phone number only; we will trace it today.'
options.outcome: A SAFE reply: say you hear her, apologize, find a secure channel, end with a next step. The sixty people who liked her comment see the bank listen, and a ticket for the digital channels team then gives the case an owner and a due time.

options.text: Reply: 'Selam, the app works fine for most customers. Please check your internet connection and try the transfer again.'
options.outcome: Blaming the customer in public angers her and everyone who agreed with her. It also ignores a transfer that may really be stuck.

options.text: Hide the comment under the moderation tool so the feature post looks better, and send Selam a private message later.
options.outcome: Criticism stays up and is answered under the moderation rules. Hiding it looks like censorship and the complaint will reappear elsewhere.

tasks.subject: Customer posts a photo of his bank statement
body: Ato Abebe Girma comments on the page with a photo of his statement, showing his full account number, balance and recent transactions, and asks why Birr 12,000 was deducted last week.
A colleague suggests answering publicly, as he shared the statement himself, so others can learn about the charge.

options.text: Hide the comment, message him privately with the reason and ask for his phone number, then route and log the query.
options.outcome: Correct. Hiding limits the exposure of his data, the private message keeps the service going, and the complaint enters the register like any branch complaint.

options.text: Reply publicly explaining the Birr 12,000 deduction, since he chose to share the statement and others may have the same question.
options.outcome: Explaining his account in public discloses his affairs to every reader. His choice to post does not give the bank a legal basis to discuss his account in public.

options.text: Leave it up and ask him to also post the transaction reference, so the account team can find the deduction quickly.
options.outcome: That adds more data to an exposure already in public. Fraudsters watch bank pages for exactly this.

options.text: Delete the comment at once to remove his account details from public view, without contacting him about it.
options.outcome: His data is protected, but he thinks the bank deleted his complaint and he still has no answer. Hide, then message him privately.

tasks.subject: Post the branch opening photos today
body: The regional director sends 20 photos of yesterday's new branch opening in Bahir Dar and asks for them to go up today. The best photo shows a customer at the counter, face clearly visible, with his passbook open in front of him. No consent forms were collected.
Several other photos show the ribbon cutting, the staff team and the outside of the branch.

options.text: Post the best photo today: he was in a public banking hall, the director chose it, and it is the strongest image of the opening.
options.outcome: A customer's face and the fact that he banks with Bank A are personal and confidential. They may be published only with written consent for the stated use.

options.text: Post the best photo with the passbook blurred out, so his account details are hidden and the director gets the image he wants.
options.outcome: Blurring the passbook does not cover his face and the fact that he is a customer. Consent is still missing.

options.text: Post today with ribbon, staff and building shots showing no customers; ask the branch for written consent for the other one.
options.outcome: Correct. The director gets the post today, and the customer's privacy is protected. Consent should name the photos, platforms and period, and he can withdraw it.

options.text: Post all 20 photos today as the director asks, and take down any photo whose customer complains about appearing in it.
options.outcome: Waiting for a complaint means the harm is already done. Consent comes before publication, not after.

tasks.subject: Post this today: 'Buy shares now, 30% dividend expected!'
body: A client company is preparing a share offer arranged by Bank A Capital, the bank's capital market subsidiary. A senior manager sends a graphic, 'Buy shares now, 30% dividend expected!', and asks you to post it on all Bank A pages today.
You can find no record that the offer has been approved, and the dividend figure is not in any approved document.

options.text: Post it today on all pages: a senior manager has asked, and Bank A Capital is a regulated subsidiary of the bank.
options.outcome: Promoting a share offer that is not approved, and promising a return, can breach the Capital Market Proclamation. Seniority does not make the post compliant.

options.text: Post it with 'terms apply, see the offer documents' at the bottom, so readers know the 30% figure is not a promise.
options.outcome: A small disclaimer does not cure an unapproved promotion or a promised dividend.

options.text: Hold it, tell the manager in writing that only an approved offer in approved wording may be promoted, and send it to compliance.
options.outcome: Correct. When the offer is approved, the desk can post it in the approved form. Until then, the page must not promote it at all.

options.text: Share it from your personal account instead, so it reaches investors without being an official Bank A post.
options.outcome: That makes it a staff conduct breach as well. Staff must not promote securities or speak for the bank from personal accounts.

tasks.from: Facebook comments and the fraud team
tasks.subject: 'I paid Birr 2,500 to your loan support channel. Where is my loan?'
body: W/ro Genet Ayana, a nurse in Adama, writes on Bank A's real page: 'I paid Birr 2,500 to your loan support channel on Telegram yesterday and nothing happened.' She includes a screenshot of the wallet number she paid. The channel, 'Bank A Loan Support', uses Bank A's logo and has 9,000 subscribers.
A colleague says the platform will take it down once reported, so there is no need for a warning post. The fraud team sends you last quarter's takedown tracker.

exhibit.title: Bank A takedown tracker, last quarter

rows.label: Total days from report to removal, for those 15
Removed fakes that reappeared under a new name

options.text: Tell her kindly it is a fake, move her to a private message, send the wallet number to fraud, report the channel and post a warning.
options.outcome: Correct. Only 15 / 20 = 75% of fakes come down, after 60 / 15 = 4 days on average, and 6 / 15 = 40% come back. Takedown alone leaves customers exposed for days, so the warning and the wallet number matter most.

options.text: Screenshot and report the channel to Telegram with the wallet number, and wait for the takedown before saying anything in public.
options.outcome: At about 4 days per takedown, thousands more subscribers can pay the fee meanwhile. Warn customers within hours of finding a new fake.

options.text: Reply publicly that Bank A will refund her Birr 2,500, so she and the other victims see that the bank stands by its customers.
options.outcome: A refund promise the desk cannot guarantee becomes the next complaint. Help her quickly in private and pass the case to the fraud team; never promise outcomes.

options.text: Reply that Bank A is not responsible for payments made to other channels, and ask customers to check the official list.
options.outcome: Blaming a victim is cruel and bad for the brand, and it misses the chance to get the wallet number to the fraud team while the money may still be traceable.

tasks.subject: 'Is the Bank A pre-listing share group real?'
body: Several customers ask on the official Telegram channel about a group selling 'Bank A pre-listing shares' at Birr 1,000 each with a promised 50% return in three months. Bank A has no share offer open. ECMA has published a general warning about unlicensed investment schemes.
A colleague wants to post the full name and photo of the person he thinks runs the group.

options.text: Warn that Bank A has no share offer open, the group is fake and no one can promise such returns; link ECMA's warning; report it.
options.outcome: Correct. Real offers come through licensed capital market service providers and approved documents. Sharing official warnings helps customers; accusing named people needs legal review.

options.text: Post the warning together with the suspected organizer's full name and photo, so customers can recognize and avoid him.
options.outcome: The warning is right, but the bank's own accusations against a named person need legal approval. If the guess is wrong, the bank has harmed an innocent person.

options.text: Say nothing: share offers belong to Bank A Capital and ECMA, not the desk, and a post might give the group more attention.
options.outcome: The scam uses Bank A's name, and customers asked the official page directly. Silence lets the group grow.

options.text: Reply that the offer may be real but carries risk, so customers should invest only what they can afford to lose.
options.outcome: Bank A has no offer open, so it is not real. Calling it 'possibly real' gives the scam the bank's credibility.

tasks.subject: A fraud warning plan for next month
body: After this week's fake channel, the manager wants a fraud warning plan for next month that follows the NBE's FCPED/142/26 model: monthly campaigns, warnings in local languages and reporting of fraud-linked numbers. Last month the page ran one fraud post, in English only.
The desk's own standard is at least one fraud post every week in each of the page's three main languages.

rows.label: Standard
rows.value: 1 fraud post per week per language

rows.label: Wallet and phone numbers reported by customers this week

options.text: A monthly theme, 4 weekly posts in 3 languages (12 versions), a refreshed pinned warning, a video, fast alerts; 7 numbers to fraud.
options.outcome: Correct: 4 x 3 = 12 versions. Regular warnings reduce fraud more than any single takedown, and passing on fraud-linked numbers follows the reporting practice in FCPED/142/26.

options.text: Four weekly fraud posts in English, the page's main language, plus a refreshed pinned warning and the 7 numbers to the fraud team.
options.outcome: Weekly is right, but English only misses many of the customers fraudsters target. The model asks for warnings in local languages.

options.text: One large fraud campaign each quarter with a video and paid boost, instead of weekly posts that customers learn to scroll past.
options.outcome: A quarterly burst leaves months without warnings while new fakes appear every week. The NBE model is monthly at least.

options.text: Reduce fraud posts to one a month, since frequent warnings scare customers away from digital banking and hurt the card campaign.
options.outcome: Customers who know the bank never asks for codes or fees trust digital channels more, not less. Silence helps only the fraudsters.

tasks.subject: A new teller's selfie shows a customer's screen
body: Scrolling Facebook, you see a public selfie posted an hour ago by a new teller at a Bank A branch, smiling at her desk. Behind her, the screen clearly shows a customer's name and balance. It already has 50 reactions and a few shares.
She is not on the digital desk, and you do not know her personally.

options.text: Comment on her post asking her politely to take it down at once, because a customer's name and balance are visible on screen.
options.outcome: A public comment draws more attention to the customer's data. Concerns go through internal channels, not into the comments.

options.text: Screenshot it, report it at once through the internal channel to her supervisor so she deletes it, and flag a data incident.
options.outcome: Correct. Do not engage, capture, report and let the owners act. Speed matters, because each share spreads the customer's details further.

options.text: Ignore it: she is not on the digital desk, personal accounts are her own business, and HR handles staff conduct.
options.outcome: Every employee is part of the early warning system, and bank secrecy applies on personal accounts too. A customer's balance is now public.

options.text: Share it in the team's group chat as a warning to colleagues of what not to post, so the same mistake is not repeated.
options.outcome: Forwarding the image spreads the customer's data further. Report it; do not circulate it.

tasks.subject: App down, 300 comments, and a card advert scheduled for 19:00
body: The mobile app has been down for 40 minutes after a system change. Digital operations confirms that balances are not affected and expects the service back by about 21:00. The page has 300 new comments, and a screenshot claiming 'Bank A is closing accounts' is spreading.
A cheerful debit card advert is scheduled for 19:00. The communications manager is at a family event but reachable by phone.

options.text: Pause the advert, call the manager, and post in three languages: app paused, money safe, ATMs and branches open, back by 21:00.
options.outcome: Correct. Silence on social media is filled by rumor, and a claim that the bank is closing is a crisis item for the manager. The notice uses plain words and only facts operations has confirmed.

options.text: Let the 19:00 card advert run as scheduled and stay quiet until the app is back, so the page does not draw attention to the outage.
options.outcome: A cheerful advert above 300 worried comments tells every visitor the bank is not listening, and the rumor spreads unanswered.

options.text: Pause the advert and reply to each of the 300 comments one by one with the same message about the outage and the fix time.
options.outcome: Kind, but slow: by the time you reach comment 300 the rumor has spread. One pinned notice, then replies pointing to it, works faster.

options.text: Post that the outage is an attack by hackers that IT is fighting, so customers know the problem is not the bank's own fault.
options.outcome: Operations said it was a system change. Guessing a cause is disinformation from the bank's own page and would cause more alarm.

followUps.subject: Selam posted her account number, and a 'Bank A Care' account replied
body: Following the agent's reply, Selam posted her full account number and the transaction ID under the public post. Ten minutes later, an account called 'BankA Care Official' replied: 'We can fix it now, send us the code you will receive by SMS.'

options.text: Hide her comment and the fake reply, warn her privately never to share the code, report the fake and alert the fraud team.
options.outcome: This stops the immediate risk. The lesson stands: never ask for details in public, because fake 'care' accounts watch for exactly these comments.

options.text: Reply under the fake account that it is not official and warn readers, and leave Selam's comment up so the team can see it.
options.outcome: The warning helps, but her account number stays public. Hide the exposed data and move her to a private channel.

options.text: Delete the whole post with all its comments, so both her account number and the fake account's reply disappear at once.
options.outcome: Deleting everything removes legitimate comments and gives Selam no warning about the code request.

followUps.subject: 'You promised my Birr 2,500 back. Where is it?'
body: The fraud team has traced the wallet but says Bank A cannot refund money paid to a third party's wallet. Genet has seen your public promise and is now posting angry comments, and others who paid the fake channel are asking for refunds too.

options.text: Apologize privately, explain what the fraud team can and cannot do, give her the case reference and correct the promise publicly.
options.outcome: Honest correction is the only way back. Never promise outcomes the desk cannot guarantee.

options.text: Ask the fraud team to pay her Birr 2,500 quietly from the complaints budget to keep her happy and stop the angry comments.
options.outcome: A quiet exception for one person while others are refused is unfair and cannot be explained to the others who paid.

options.text: Stop replying to her messages and hide her new comments, since the fraud team has already said no refund is possible.
options.outcome: Silence turns a broken promise into a public dispute. She needs an honest answer.

followUps.subject: 'Bank A closing accounts' is trending
body: The app came back at 21:10, but the page posted nothing. The 'closing accounts' screenshot has been shared thousands of times overnight, and branches report customers queuing to withdraw cash this morning.

options.text: Post and pin a notice in three languages: accounts are safe, the app was back at 21:10; give branches the same words.
options.outcome: Fast, factual and consistent messages across every channel are how a rumor fades. Next time, the first notice goes out within minutes.

options.text: Delete the comments that share the screenshot and turn off comments on the page until the queues at branches calm down.
options.outcome: Deleting looks like hiding and confirms the rumor for many readers.

options.text: Wait until Monday for IT's full incident report, so the bank's statement is complete and cannot be questioned later.
options.outcome: Customers are queuing now. The facts you need, accounts safe and service restored, are already known.

memo.prompt: Write your end-of-week hand-over note to the communications manager.
guide: On-time reply rate, unanswered comments and complaints logged this week against the three goals.
Fake accounts found, reported and removed, and the numbers passed to the fraud team.
Posts you paused or refused, and what approval or consent each still needs.
One process change that would have prevented the week's biggest problem.

exam.q: A bank's app is down on a Saturday and comments are piling up. What should the page do first?
options: Wait until the fix is complete, then post
Turn off comments until Monday
Post a short, calm notice saying what is affected, that money is safe if confirmed, and when the next update will come
Post a product advert to change the subject
exam.explain: A quick, honest notice stops rumour from filling the silence; the claim that money is safe must be confirmed first.

exam.q: A fake Telegram channel uses Bank A's name. Which single measure best helps customers tell real from fake over time?
options: A published official list of accounts and contact numbers on the website and pages
A new logo
More adverts
Closing the bank's own Telegram channel
exam.explain: If an account is not on the official list, it is not the bank.

exam.q: A page received 800 comments needing a reply, and 560 were answered within one hour. The target is 80%. By how many replies did it miss the target?
exam.explain: 80% of 800 is 640; 640 minus 560 is 80 replies short.

exam.q: Hiwot finds a scheduled post with last quarter's interest rate. The new rate is not yet confirmed in writing. What should she do?
options: Post on time and fix later
Pause the post and reschedule once the approved rate is confirmed in writing
Use the rate she heard in a meeting
Remove the rate and say "attractive rates"
exam.explain: Rates must match the approved tariff before publication; a vague claim can also mislead.

exam.q: A monthly plan has 40 posts, of which 22 are product adverts. What is the product share, and is it within Bank A's guidance of under a third?
options: 35%, within guidance
55%, above guidance
45%, above guidance
22%, within guidance
exam.explain: 22 divided by 40 is 55%, well above one third.

exam.q: Which post most likely breaches capital market rules?
options: A link to an official ECMA warning
A branch opening notice
A savings tip video
"Buy our subsidiary's shares now, 30% dividend expected" before any approved offer
exam.explain: Promoting an unapproved offer and promising returns can breach the Capital Market Proclamation.

exam.q: A customer story video shows a customer's loan agreement in the background. She consented to her photo, first name and business name only. What should the desk do?
options: Remove or reshoot the frame so the agreement is not visible before publishing
Publish, since she consented to appear
Publish and blur it later if she complains
Ask her to consent to the loan details afterwards
exam.explain: Consent covered named items only; loan details are confidential.

exam.q: Two posts: A reached 40,000 with 1,600 engagements; B reached 25,000 with 1,250. Which has the higher engagement rate?
options: Both 4%

exam.q: A customer posts a photo of her statement with her account number. What is the correct first action?
options: Explain her transactions in a public reply
Delete it without telling her
Leave it, since she posted it herself
Hide the comment, explain why in a private message and move her to a secure channel
exam.explain: Hiding limits exposure; telling her why keeps trust and service going.

exam.q: Which reply follows the SAFE method?
options: "Our records show no error."
"Selam, sorry your card has not arrived after two weeks. Please message us your phone number and our card team will call you today."
"Please post your card number so we can check."
"Read our terms and conditions."
exam.explain: It says we hear you, apologises, finds a secure channel and ends with a next step.

exam.q: Under the published moderation rules, which comment should be removed?
options: "Your service is the slowest in town."
"I waited two hours at the branch today."
A comment with a phone number claiming to be the bank's loan desk, which is not on the official list
"Why are your fees higher this year?"
exam.explain: Fake contact numbers are scam content; criticism stays and is answered.

exam.q: A journalist tags the bank asking about a viral video of a branch incident. What should the duty agent do?
options: Alert the communications manager at once and not reply alone
Reply with their own view
Ignore it
Ask the journalist for their account number
exam.explain: Media, regulator and viral incident posts escalate straight to management.

exam.q: Bank A received 500 social media complaints and logged 200 in the register. What share went unlogged, and why does it matter?
options: 40%, it does not matter if solved
60%, but logging is optional for social media
20%, only for platform reasons
60%, management cannot see root causes and complaint reports understate the problem
exam.explain: 300 of 500, or 60%, went unlogged; social media complaints belong in the complaint procedure.

exam.q: Which feature is the strongest sign that an account is fake?
options: It has many followers
It asks for a fee into a personal mobile wallet to release a loan
It posts in Amharic
It uses the bank's colours
exam.explain: Real banks do not collect loan fees into personal wallets.

exam.q: In one quarter, 30 fakes were found, 21 removed, and removal took 126 days in total. What are the removal rate and average days to removal?
options: 70% and 4.2 days
70% and 6 days
63% and 6 days
21% and 6 days

exam.q: Which description of NBE Instruction FCPED/142/26 is accurate?
options: It requires banks to close Telegram channels
It sets interest rates for digital loans
It sets the minimum capital of microfinance institutions
It requires microfinance institutions to run monthly fraud awareness campaigns, warn in local languages, report fraud-linked numbers and accounts, and report to the NBE within 10 days
exam.explain: That is the instruction's scope; banks can use it as a model.

exam.q: A scam victim says he paid 2,500 Birr to a fake loan channel. What matters most in the first hour?
options: Getting the receiving wallet number and details to the fraud team fast
Explaining publicly that it was his fault
Promising a refund
Deleting his comment
exam.explain: Speed can help stop funds moving and helps block the wallet.

exam.q: A staff member knows a listed company's results before publication and hints on Facebook that friends should buy its shares. What is the main issue?
options: Only a brand voice problem
None, if the post is on a personal account
Possible insider dealing or market abuse under the Capital Market Proclamation and a breach of staff policy
A data protection issue only
exam.explain: Passing on inside information before it is public can breach capital market rules.

exam.q: A forwarded video in a staff group insults an ethnic group and makes an unproven claim about a branch. What should a staff member do?
options: Forward it with a disclaimer
Post it publicly to expose it
Reply with counter-insults
Not forward it, ask that it be deleted, and report it under the staff policy
exam.explain: Forwarding spreads possible hate speech and disinformation; reporting is the right path.

exam.q: In the feed simulation, a learner writes a warm, accurate reply but asks the customer to post a transaction ID in public. How is that post scored?
options: Full marks, because tone and accuracy are good
Its score is capped because of the compliance failure
Only tone points are lost
It is not scored
exam.explain: A compliance failure caps the post's score, because public disclosure risks outweigh good tone.
